subject: Chemistry
title: Solutions
summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture. Its concentration can be written as mass %, ppm, mole fraction, molarity or molality.

Gases dissolve more at higher pressure (Henry's law) and usually less at higher temperature. For volatile liquids, Raoult's law says each component's vapour pressure = its mole fraction × its pure vapour pressure.
Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law exactly; real ones show positive deviation (weaker A–B attractions) or negative deviation (stronger A–B attractions) and may form azeotropes.

Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles: relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure. The van't Hoff factor i corrects for dissociation or association.

formulas.name: Henry's law
formulas.formula: p = K_H x  (partial pressure ∝ mole fraction of gas in solution)
formulas.note: A larger K_H means LOWER solubility at the same pressure.

formulas.name: Raoult's law (volatile components)
formulas.formula: p_A = x_A p°_A;  p_total = x_A p°_A + x_B p°_B

formulas.name: Vapour composition
formulas.when: Mole fraction of a component in the vapour.
formulas.note: The vapour is richer in the MORE volatile component.

formulas.name: Boiling-point elevation
formulas.mistake: m is molality (per kg solvent), not molarity.

formulas.name: Freezing-point depression
formulas.formula: ΔT_f = i K_f m;  water K_f = 1.86, K_b = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹

formulas.name: Osmotic pressure
formulas.formula: π = i C R T  (C in mol/L, R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
formulas.when: Osmosis, molar mass of polymers and proteins.

formulas.name: Molar mass from colligative data
formulas.formula: M₂ = (K_b × w₂ × 1000)/(ΔT_b × w₁)  (similarly with K_f);  M₂ = w₂RT/(πV)
formulas.when: Finding the molar mass of a solute.

formulas.name: van't Hoff factor
formulas.formula: i = observed colligative property / normal value = normal molar mass / observed molar mass

formulas.name: i from dissociation or association
formulas.formula: dissociation into n ions: i = 1 + (n − 1)α;  association into n-mers: i = 1 − (1 − 1/n)α

examples.title: Ideal mixture
examples.problem: Benzene (p° = 75 torr) and toluene (p° = 22 torr), x = 0.5 each. Total vapour pressure and mole fraction of benzene in the vapour?

examples.title: Lowering of vapour pressure
examples.problem: Pure water p° = 23.8 mm Hg. Solute mole fraction 0.02 (non-volatile, non-electrolyte). Lowering?

examples.title: Molar mass from osmotic pressure
examples.problem: 1.8 g of a solute in 250 mL of solution gives π = 0.738 atm at 300 K. Molar mass?

examples.title: Association of acetic acid
examples.problem: Acetic acid (M = 60) shows an apparent molar mass of 100 in benzene. Degree of association?

topics.title: Types of solutions
topics.explain: Solvent and solute can be any phase: gas in liquid (soda), solid in liquid (sugar), liquid in liquid (alcohol in water), solid in solid (alloys), gas in solid (H₂ in palladium).

topics.title: Solubility of solids and gases
topics.explain: Solids: 'like dissolves like'; solubility usually rises with temperature if dissolution is endothermic. Gases: solubility rises with pressure (Henry's law) and falls with temperature — fish need cold water, and divers get the bends when dissolved N₂ bubbles out.

topics.title: Ideal and non-ideal solutions
topics.explain: Ideal (benzene + toluene): ΔmixH = 0, ΔmixV = 0. Positive deviation (ethanol + acetone, CS₂ + acetone): weaker A–B forces, ΔmixH > 0, ΔmixV > 0, minimum-boiling azeotrope. Negative deviation (chloroform + acetone, HNO₃ + water): stronger A–B forces, ΔmixH < 0, ΔmixV < 0, maximum-boiling azeotrope.

topics.title: Azeotropes
topics.explain: Constant-boiling mixtures that cannot be separated by simple distillation, e.g. 95% ethanol–water (minimum boiling) and 68% HNO₃–water (maximum boiling).

topics.title: Osmosis and reverse osmosis
topics.explain: Solvent moves through a semipermeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution. Isotonic solutions have the same π (0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood); RBCs swell in hypotonic and shrink in hypertonic solutions. Applying pressure greater than π reverses the flow — used to desalinate sea water.

topics.title: Abnormal molar masses
topics.explain: Electrolytes dissociate (i > 1) and give lower apparent molar mass; solutes like acetic acid in benzene associate (i < 1) and give higher apparent molar mass.

ratta: Henry: p = K_H x (higher K_H → less soluble).
Raoult: p_A = x_A p°_A;  vapour richer in volatile one.
Δp/p° = x₂;  ΔT_b = iK_b m;  ΔT_f = iK_f m;  π = iCRT.
